title: The assistant that promised free rebooking
scenario:
You are head of digital at an online travel agency with 600 staff. Your website assistant runs on Anthropic's API through a workspace API key called web-assistant. Last night something went wrong.

The CEO calls you at 09:30 and asks what to do first. The exhibit shows the log and three proposals from the team.
exhibit:
Incident INC-7: website assistant (made-up example data)

Timeline (Tuesday)
  02:10  Spend alert: day spend 3x a normal day. Sent to dev-alerts@
         (no owner; last read 3 weeks ago).
  08:40  Customer form: "The assistant promised me free rebooking."
  09:15  Review: 38 answers offered discounts we never sell.
         One visitor account sent 4,000 requests overnight, many
         telling the assistant to ignore its rules.

Facts
  - Key web-assistant is a workspace key created in the Console.
  - Workspace "Production" also runs the booking-email tool.
  - All requests go out under one key, with no per-user identifier.

Proposals
  P1  Remove developer Sam from the organization (he made the key).
  P2  Archive the whole "Production" workspace.
  P3  Add to the prompt: "Never invent discounts."

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness in how this incident was spotted?

options.text: The spend alert did not exist, so nothing could have warned the team.
options.explanation: The exhibit shows an alert at 02:10. The alert worked.

options.text: The alert went to an address no one owns, so no person read it for hours.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's safety guide says a report method should be monitored by a human. The same holds for alerts: a named person must read them.

options.text: The alert was set too low, so it fired on a day with normal spend.
options.explanation: The exhibit says spend was 3 times a normal day. The alert fired for a real reason.

options.text: The customer form was the wrong place to report problems about the assistant.
options.explanation: A report form is what the safety guides recommend. The form worked at 08:40.

questions.prompt: Which containment step fits best at 09:30?

options.text: P1. Removing Sam stops the web-assistant key, so the problem ends at once.
options.explanation: Anthropic's Admin API page says workspace API keys continue to work when a user is removed. P1 may stop nothing.

options.text: P2. Archive the "Production" workspace, so every key in it stops at once.
options.explanation: Archiving archives every key in the workspace, cannot be undone, and would also stop the booking-email tool.

options.text: Set the key to inactive, show a fixed FAQ page, and lower the workspace limits.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's Admin API can change a key's status, and workspace limits can be set lower. This is the smallest step that stops the harm and can be undone.

options.text: Leave the assistant on until the cause is known, so customers keep getting help.
options.explanation: Containment comes before the investigation. Every hour of delay means more invented discounts.

questions.prompt: One visitor account sent 4,000 rule-breaking requests. Which step fits the vendors' guidance?

options.text: Throttle or block that account, and tag requests with a per-user identifier from now on.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's jailbreak guide says to consider throttling or banning repeat offenders. Anthropic's Messages API has a metadata user_id field to help detect abuse; OpenAI's safety guide recommends safety identifiers for the same reason.

options.text: Send an email to all customers asking them not to try to break the assistant.
options.explanation: This does not stop the one account, and it tells the other visitors about an attack they did not know about.

options.text: Take no action against the account, because it only sent text and cannot act.
options.explanation: The vendor guide says to respond to repeat offenders. The same attacker can keep trying until a prompt works.

options.text: Block every visitor who has not logged in, and keep the block in place for good.
options.explanation: That is far wider than the problem. It punishes all new customers because of one account.

questions.prompt: The team wants to close the incident with P3 only. What should the "learn" step include instead?

options.text: Find who set up the alert address, and write a formal warning for their file.
options.explanation: The lesson says to keep the write-up about the system, not a person. Blame makes people hide the next problem.

options.text: Move to another AI vendor, because the attack shows this vendor is unsafe.
options.explanation: The weak points were the alert owner, key handling and testing. A new vendor would have the same gaps.

options.text: Keep P3 as the only change, because a clear prompt rule makes the model safe to use.
options.explanation: A prompt line helps, but both vendors' guides say to test with attacks and add other controls. A prompt alone does not remove the risk.

options.text: Add the attack messages to the red-team tests, name an alert owner, fix the policy.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI and Anthropic both recommend red-teaming, and the lesson says to fix the rule that failed.
